paragraphs.text: [Nanqiao](nanqiao-ruigong-brick:nanqiao-name) was once the name of the county around Mengzhe in southern Yunnan. Menghai County Nanqiao Tea Company, founded in February 2004, kept that old name for itself. The China Tea Marketing Association lists Che Fo Nan as its brand and records that its teas went to Hong Kong, Taiwan and Southeast Asia. Ruigong bricks reached that trade: at a Malaysian tea fair in 2022, the exhibitor Quanyuxuan offered five of them together at stall 27, listed as [ripe tea from 2008](nanqiao-ruigong-brick:malaysian-tea-fair), a year older than this one.

This brick holds leaf from [Menghai County](menghai-county:county-and-factory), made into [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) in 2009. The leaf was heaped warm and damp in a [fermenting pile](shou:wet-piling) and turned so that air could reach it, all to give in weeks the dark cup that raw pu’er takes years to reach. Yunnan’s state factories brought that method into production in 1973, so this brick comes from the style’s fourth decade.

At seventeen years it is well past the ten that the trade counts as [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged). The leaf keeps changing slowly with the air and moisture around it, which is why the way it has been kept matters as much as its years.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.
